h1: The 6 Best Printers for High-Volume Printing of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six printers built for heavy monthly page counts, from compact mono lasers to refillable ink tanks, with who each suits.
summary: The Canon MF753Cdw II is the best high-volume printer here: 35 ppm, a document feeder and a three-year warranty. The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the pick for text-only offices, and the Epson ET-4950 is the cheapest way to print color at scale. The HP Smart Tank 5101 and Epson ET-4800 handle tighter budgets, with real tradeoffs in feeder and design age.
intro: Printer pricing is a shell game. The machine on the shelf is often subsidized, and the maker earns the difference back through toner, ink and drum replacements for the next three years. That is why a bargain unit can quietly become the most expensive object in a busy office, and why a heavier, pricier laser can end up the cheaper tool at 3,000 pages a month.

Our six picks split into two camps: fast laser engines built for shared queues, and refillable tank inkjets built for cheap color. We reviewed each on engine type, rated speed, paper handling, running-cost design and warranty, then ranked them on the Primea framework. Speed and duty design carried the most weight, because volume punishes slow, fussy machines first.

products.name: Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II Wireless Duplex Laser Printer
products.verdict: The fastest and sturdiest machine here for offices that never stop printing.
products.description:
The Canon MF753Cdw II is a color laser rated at 35 pages per minute, and it bundles an automatic document feeder, duplex printing, fax, copy and scan. That combination matters at volume: a feeder lets one person scan a stack unattended, and duplex halves paper use on every long job. A three-year limited warranty is the longest coverage in this group.

It beats the Brother HL-L3220CDW, at 19 ppm, by a wide margin. A 500-page job that takes about 14 minutes on the Canon takes closer to 26 on the Brother. The Epson tanks trail further, at 18 ppm, though they print color more cheaply per page.

Buy it for a shared office that prints color all day. The caveat is footprint: it is the largest machine in the ranking, and laser toner for color gets expensive at low volume, so skip it under a few hundred pages a month.
products.idealFor: Busy shared offices that print in color all day.
products.skipIf: You print a few hundred pages a month or have a tight desk.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser
products.verdict: A compact black-and-white workhorse for text-heavy volume.
products.description:
The Brother DCP-L2640DW is a monochrome laser with automatic duplex, copy and scan, wireless and mobile printing, and a compact body built for sustained use. Dropping color removes the costliest part of a laser's consumables, which is why text-heavy offices running invoices, contracts and reports tend to see the lowest cost per page from mono engines.

It sits behind the Canon because it gives up color, the faster rated engine and fax. Against the HL-L3220CDW below, it is the smarter buy if color never appears in your workflow, since you are not paying for toner you will not use.

Choose it for a legal, accounting or admin desk. The limit is blunt: any client chart or branded handout must be outsourced, and the listing shows no fax, so check before replacing an old fax line.
products.idealFor: Text-heavy offices that never need color.
products.skipIf: You print marketing material or charts.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-4950 Wireless Cartridge-Free Supertank Printer
products.verdict: Refillable tanks that keep color cheap over thousands of pages.
products.description:
The Epson EcoTank ET-4950 swaps cartridges for refillable ink tanks, rated for up to three years of ink refills, and adds an automatic document feeder and a 2.4-inch color touchscreen. Tank systems move the economics: bottled ink costs far less per page than cartridges, and color stops being a luxury line item.

It lands third because 18 ppm cannot keep up with the Canon or a big queue. What it does beat is every laser here on the cost of a color page. Against the ET-4800 below, the touchscreen and longer rated ink supply justify stepping up.

Pick it for a color-heavy shop that prints steadily rather than in bursts, such as a design or real estate office. The caveat is refilling: bottles are messier than swapping a toner cartridge, and fast bursts of pages are not its strength.
products.idealFor: Color-heavy shops wanting the lowest running cost.
products.skipIf: You need fast bursts or mostly black text.

products.name: Brother Color Laser Printer HL-L3220CDW
products.verdict: A modest color laser for steady volume without the Canon bulk.
products.description:
The Brother HL-L3220CDW is a color laser at 19 ppm with automatic duplex, a 250-sheet tray and wireless and mobile printing. It is print-only, with no scanner or feeder, which keeps the machine smaller and cheaper than the Canon while still giving you laser-sharp text and color.

It ranks fourth because it trails the Canon on speed by nearly half and lacks any scan function. Compared with the mono DCP-L2640DW above, you pay for color capability that only earns its keep if clients or marketing work need it regularly.

It suits an office that prints color documents in moderate runs and handles scanning elsewhere. The 250-sheet tray is the practical limit: heavy days mean frequent refills, so this is not the machine for a queue that never stops.
products.idealFor: Offices needing regular color without a big machine.
products.skipIf: You also need scanning or a document feeder.

products.name: HP Smart Tank 5101 Wireless All-in-One Refillable Printer
products.verdict: A small tank printer that ships with two years of ink.
products.description:
The HP Smart Tank 5101 is a compact refillable ink tank all-in-one that ships with about two years of ink and prints, scans and copies over 2.4GHz Wi-Fi. Bundling that much ink at a low entry price makes the first two years of color unusually cheap, and it takes less desk space than larger tank models.

It ranks below both Epson tanks because it has no automatic document feeder, so every multi-page scan or copy becomes a manual page-by-page job. The Epsons also offer faster paths to scanning stacks. The size trade is real, though, since the HP is the smallest tank machine here.

Best for a home office or small team that prints color on a budget but scans single pages. The sharper caveat is Wi-Fi: it joins only 2.4GHz networks, so check your router band before ordering.
products.idealFor: Small offices wanting cheap color on a budget.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-4800 Wireless Cartridge-Free Supertank Printer
products.verdict: Older but capable tank printer with Ethernet and fax.
products.description:
The Epson EcoTank ET-4800 uses the same cartridge-free tank approach as the ET-4950 but adds Ethernet alongside Wi-Fi, plus fax, an automatic document feeder, scanner and copier. Wired networking matters in shared offices, where wireless drops under load can stall a print queue mid-job.

It closes the list because the ET-4950 is the newer design with a touchscreen and a longer rated ink supply. The ET-4800 is the cheaper way into tank economics, and it beats the HP Smart Tank 5101 on feeder and Ethernet, though it sits in the same price bucket.

Choose it for a budget office scaling up to heavy printing that wants a wired connection and fax. The caveat is age: it is an older model with fewer conveniences, and no touchscreen.
products.idealFor: Budget offices wanting wired network printing.
products.skipIf: You want a touchscreen or the longest ink supply.

methodology.description: We compared laser and refillable tank designs, since each suits different page mixes.

methodology.title: Rated speed
methodology.description: We used published pages per minute as a rough guide to how fast a large queue clears.

methodology.title: Running-cost model
methodology.description: We looked at how each machine delivers ink or toner and what it implies for long-term cost.

methodology.description: We checked duplex, tray size and document feeders for multi-page work.

methodology.title: Warranty and support
methodology.description: We noted listed warranty terms and connectivity options such as Ethernet.

whatMatters.detail: Engine type decides almost everything else. Laser printers fuse toner with heat and excel at fast, crisp text. Tank inkjets spray liquid ink from refillable reservoirs and print color far more cheaply per page. The Canon and Brother models here are lasers, the Epson and HP ones are tanks. Confirm the word laser or tank in the title before comparing anything else.

Rated speed is pages per minute, and it determines how long a stack ties up the machine. At 18 ppm, a 500-page job runs about 28 minutes; at the Canon's 35 ppm, about 14. Find the ppm figure in the spec bullets, and remember it is a best-case number for plain black text, not photos.

Ink and toner economics decide the real price of ownership. Refillable tanks and high-yield cartridges lower the cost per page, while cheap cartridge machines recover their discount through refills. At high volume the consumables bill dwarfs the purchase price. Look for tank, high-yield or included-ink wording in the listing, such as the HP's two years of ink.

Paper handling is duplex plus feeder. Automatic duplex prints both sides and halves paper use. An automatic document feeder lets you copy or scan a stack without standing at the glass. The Canon and the Epsons include feeders; the HL-L3220CDW and HP 5101 do not. Check that both features are named in the listing, not implied.

Warranty and connectivity signal how the maker expects the machine to be used. A three-year limited warranty, like the Canon's, suggests duty-cycle confidence. Ethernet keeps a shared printer stable when Wi-Fi congests, as on the ET-4800. Look for the warranty length and the word Ethernet in the spec list before buying for multiple users.

faq.q: Is a laser or ink tank printer better for high volume?
faq.a: Laser wins on speed and plain text, which is why the Canon MF753Cdw II and Brother DCP-L2640DW lead. Tank printers like the Epson ET-4950 win on the cost of color. Decide by your page mix, not just by monthly volume.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when buying one?
faq.a: Judging by machine price alone. Consumables dominate cost within a couple of years, so check whether a model uses toner, high-yield cartridges or refillable tanks. The HP Smart Tank 5101 even ships with about two years of ink included.

faq.q: Is the Canon worth it over the Brother color laser?
faq.a: If you print constantly, yes. The Canon rates 35 ppm against the Brother HL-L3220CDW's 19, and its feeder saves scanning time. For modest color runs without scanning, the Brother covers the job at a lower footprint.

faq.q: How do I set up a shared printer?
faq.a: Use Ethernet where the model has it, such as the Epson ET-4800, and assign the printer a fixed address so users never lose it. Wi-Fi works on the Canon and Brother lasers, but wired links hold up better under shared load.

faq.q: How do I maintain a tank printer?
faq.a: Refill tanks with the matching bottles before they run dry, and print a page weekly so nozzles do not clog. On the Epson ET-4950 and HP Smart Tank 5101, avoid letting ink fall to the bottom of the tank.

faq.q: Does the HP Smart Tank work on 5GHz Wi-Fi?
faq.a: No. The listing says 2.4GHz only, so a router running only a 5GHz band will not connect it. Check your network settings first, or use the Epson ET-4800 with Ethernet if your office network is awkward.

finalTake: The Canon MF753Cdw II is the right call when several people print color all day. Text-only offices should pick the Brother DCP-L2640DW and stop paying for color toner. Color on a tighter budget points to the Epson ET-4950, and the ET-4800 or HP 5101 when price matters most. Match the engine to your page mix before anything else.
